paragraphs.text: All seven weekdays are masculine nouns, but in speech you almost never meet the article standing on its own, because a day does not stand alone. It hides inside a small word that means at, so you meet it fused into one piece.
an dem Montag → am Montag · an dem Sonntag → am Sonntag
That fusion explains why {{de:am}} is worth learning as one unit with the day behind it. Ask {{de:Wann?}} and every answer in this chapter arrives with {{de:am}} in front of it.

The list also runs in a fixed order that never changes, and the last two days are the ones your week is built around — the work days finish on {{de:Freitag}} and the free days are {{de:Samstag}} and {{de:Sonntag}}.
Montag · Dienstag · Mittwoch · Donnerstag · Freitag · Samstag · Sonntag
Two friends want to meet and the first suggestion does not fit. Read the exchange once for its shape: an offer, an acceptance, a day proposed, a polite refusal, another day, a yes.
Notice how short every line is — three or four words, no full sentence needed. The day always sits behind {{de:am}}, which is why {{de:Wann?}} is the question that gets this conversation moving.
Gehen wir ins Kino? — Ja, gern. Wann?

paragraphs.text: German has one written word for no, but spoken German is kinder to the person being refused. In the north you will hear {{de:nee}}, in Bavaria and Austria {{de:na}}, and {{de:nö}} is common across the middle of the country. All three mean exactly the same thing.

The word doing the real work is {{de:leider}} — unfortunately. It changes nothing about the answer, but it tells the other person you are sorry to say it, so a bare {{de:nein}} without it comes across harder than you meant.
A refusal usually hands the conversation straight back with a second day attached, and that is what keeps an appointment alive instead of killing it.
Am Samstag? — Nein. Am Mittwoch? — Ja, super.
